text: Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (invasive ductal carcinoma) shows malignant epithelial cells infiltrating the stroma in nests, cords, and tubules, and is the most common invasive breast cancer.
Invasive lobular carcinoma classically grows as single-file cords of small, discohesive cells infiltrating the stroma, often in a targetoid pattern around residual ducts.
Loss of membranous E-cadherin expression is characteristic of invasive lobular carcinoma and reflects the discohesive growth caused by CDH1 inactivation, distinguishing it from ductal carcinoma.
Ductal carcinoma in situ is a non-invasive proliferation of malignant epithelial cells confined within the ductal-lobular system by an intact myoepithelial layer and basement membrane.

Invasive breast carcinomas are graded by the Nottingham system, summing scores for tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic count; high nuclear grade tumours show marked pleomorphism and brisk mitoses.
Benign breast tissue and fibrocystic change retain organised ducts and lobules with a preserved two-cell layer (epithelial plus outer myoepithelial cells) and no stromal invasion.
